title: VB9-00760
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal by XXXX XXXX XXXX (Ms. F). After independently reviewing the record I find that the Refugee Protection Division's (RPD) decision is correct, and that Ms. F is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

Ms. F is a Tanzanian citizen who claimed protection in Canada so that she could escape an abusive husband. In 2003, Ms. F met XXXX. When he later asked to marry her, she accepted, and he paid a dowry of XXXX XXXX Tanzanian shillings to her parents. They were married in XXXX 2004 and for several months afterward, their relationship was great. Around XXXX of that year, XXXX began to be physically and sexually abusive, forcing Ms. F to engage in sexual acts that were forbidden or considered shameful in her Muslim faith. Sometimes Ms. F would run to her parents' home for relief but she was never permitted to stay since she was not divorced, and a married woman's place was supposed to be next to her husband. In addition to the physical abuse, Ms. F was financially controlled. She was a housewife and only received grocery money from her husband. Ms. F never reported any of the abuse to the police. She did not try to divorce her husband because her family would have had to pay back the dowry they received, and they could not do so. This meant that the only path to divorce was if her husband asked for one. In XXXX 2017, XXXX told Ms. F that they were going to go to Canada for one week. She dropped their two children off with her parents and they came to Canada. One day, when she was apart from him, Ms. F seized the opportunity and ran. With the help of strangers, she was able to travel from Toronto to Winnipeg, and there was assisted in finding shelter and making her refugee claim.

Ms. F's claim was heard over two sittings in November 2018, with the Minister intervening through written submissions. Her claim was rejected on January 3, 2019, because the RPD found that some of her core allegations were not credible. Specifically, the RPD found that Ms. F was not credible in her testimony about the circumstances of her married life, her family's impoverishment, or her reasons for being unable to obtain a divorce. The RPD also found that there were significant inconsistencies between Ms. F's narrative and the affidavits from her brother and father. Finally, the RPD found that Ms. F's testimony was evasive or simply non-responsive. Arguments on appeal

Ms. F argues that the RPD erred by disregarding the impact that her limited education had on her testimony. She argues that the RPD applied the wrong standard to determine the plausibility of Ms. F's narrative, and that the RPD failed to consider the country conditions evidence regarding domestic violence in Tanzania. Finally, Ms. F argues that the RPD did not properly apply the Gender Guideline.1

Ms. F has neither introduced new evidence nor requested an oral hearing. ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD) [1] I have applied the standard of correctness while reviewing the RPD decision and have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence before me.

For the reasons that follow, I find that the RPD's decision is correct and that Ms. F is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The determinative issue is the credibility of core elements of Ms. F's evidence, the concerns around which were not reasonably explained, including by cultural or other barriers to testimony. Application of the Gender Guideline

Ms. F raised three arguments regarding the RPD's application of the Gender Guideline to her claim. The first argument relates to the need for cross-cultural competency. The Gender Guideline instructs decision-makers to approach the evidence with cultural sensitivity, recognizing that in some instances marital dignity is a cultural norm that encourages women to be secretive about sexual violence since it is considered shameful and a stain on the honour of the family.2

Although Ms. F highlights this portion of the Gender Guideline, she does not explain how that applies to the RPD's assessment of her evidence. I note that the RPD did not ask inappropriate questions about the nature of the sexual abuse that she experienced. All of the details that were provided were volunteered, and sometimes given against clear instructions by her own counsel that such detail was not necessary. Against that backdrop, and considering that the RPD did not draw negative credibility inferences from a lack of detail about sexual violence, I do not find that his argument has merit. I find that the RPD did not err in its treatment of Ms. F's testimony regarding sexual violence.

Secondly, Ms. F argues that the RPD's failure to apply the Gender Guideline is evident in its repeated use of the word 'allegation' to describe her evidence. I agree that the word, when repeated often, can reflect an unwillingness to treat testimony as truthful. However, I have reviewed the evidence and transcripts of the hearings and find that, considered in its totality, that is not how the RPD was treating Ms. F's evidence. I do not find that the RPD erred by referring at times to Ms. F's evidence as allegations.

Finally, Ms. F points to the recognition in the Guidelines that women who have experienced sexual violence may exhibit symptoms of Rape Trauma Syndrome or Battered Woman Syndrome, and states that the RPD ought to have asked whether this may have caused Ms. F's problems with testifying.3 I note, however, that Ms. F does not point to any clear examples where this consideration ought to have changed the RPD's assessment of her testimony.

Nevertheless, it is obvious from the RPD's decision and the transcript of the hearing,4 that there was a point in Ms. F's testimony where her credibility was considerably challenged. This was the point, during her second hearing, where Ms. F stated that she had gone to Thailand in 2016 with her husband, and that they had not needed childcare because she had no children at the time. The RPD immediately contradicted this, pointing out to Ms. F that her children were born in 2010 and 2012. Shortly after this point counsel began stating that Ms. F was not behaving normally, and although she said she was stressed, Ms. F stated that she was fine. After calling a twenty-minute break to give Ms. F time to recover and to speak with her counsel, the hearing resumed. Ms. F again indicated that she was fine but had not slept well the previous night. She then explained that she had asked her parents to watch her children during that trip to Thailand, which was the only time she left Dar es Salaam before coming to Canada.

There is no evidence before me to suggest that Ms. F would have problems testifying because of any psychological reason or disorder, including effects of Battered Woman Syndrome or Rape Trauma Syndrome. In the absence of such evidence, it would be speculative for me to conclude that a psychological barrier caused Ms. F's failure to recall the existence of her children in 2016 or that she had taken them to stay with her parents during her trip to Thailand.

Ms. F's definitive statement that she did not have children in 2016 is concerning, as is her failure to recall the first and only other time that she had to ask her parents to watch her children. The fact that her trip to Thailand was her first time leaving Dar es Salaam is also significant because it means that this trip was memorable for two reasons: it was her first journey outside of her city, and the first time she left her children in the care of others. I agree with the RPD that this makes the event noteworthy.

Based on my review of the transcript and evidence, I see no reason to disturb the RPD's negative credibility finding based on her claims of having never had her parents watch her children until she left for Canada. I note that this is not a situation where Ms. F confused dates or events because she had experienced multiple similar incidents. I also note that Ms. F was consistent in stating, during both hearings, that she had never left her children with anyone, for even a short period, until she left Tanzania for Canada. I find that Ms. F is not credible in her testimony on this issue. Ms. F's education does not affect her testimony

Ms. F has argued that the RPD did not consider her limited education when assessing her credibility.5 Although she notes that the RPD mentioned her primary school education and its comments that she did not appear "sophisticated or astute"6 she states that this is not the same as being uneducated, and argues that the problems which the RPD attributed to vague testimony can be attributed to a lack of education.

The Gender Guideline stresses that decision-makers should be aware of a claimant's social, cultural, economic and religious context in order to assess the reasonableness of her actions, or plausibility of her narrative.7 In applying that guidance to my assessment of Ms. F's testimony, I am mindful that much of her testimony was about her and her family's sources of income, the people responsible for the care of her children, her education, reasons for being unable to obtain a divorce, and her travels. With the exception of her knowledge about travel documents and legal divorce processes, I do not find that responses to these questions about Ms. F's lived experience would require a great deal of education to answer. I agree with the RPD that Ms. F ought to have been able to provide detailed and clear testimony about her personal life.

Ms. F has not provided any specific examples of how her lack of education could be used to explain what the RPD found to be vague testimony. I have reviewed the RPD's credibility findings stemming from vague testimony about her training as a XXXX and her family's impoverishment. I note that the RPD's findings were not based solely on vague testimony but contradictions and inconsistencies as well. Ms. F has not challenged those grounds of the RPD's findings.

Based on my own independent review, I see no error in the RPD's credibility findings about Ms. F's evidence regarding her and her family's impoverishment, or about Ms. F's training as a XXXX. I find that Ms. F lacks credibility on both counts and find, on a balance of probabilities, that Ms. F was not impoverished and that she did not attend a XXXX course in Tanzania. The RPD applied the correct test to determine plausibility

Ms. F argues that the RPD applied the incorrect standard of balance of probabilities to its plausibility findings. Based on my independent review, I find that the RPD was assessing the credibility of Ms. F's circumstances and explanations for contradictions and inconsistencies on the basis of what is possible or could reasonably be expected for her to know. Although the RPD did not explicitly refer to the standard that Ms. F identifies, which is whether there is no reasonable possibility that events could have happened as described, I find that the RPD did not apply a higher standard to its assessment. As a result, I find that the RPD did not err. The impact of country conditions evidence on Ms. F's testimony

Ms. F has argued that the RPD did not consider the country conditions evidence speaking to police corruption and how that forms a barrier to reporting domestic violence. While I do not dispute the accuracy of that evidence, I do not find it particularly relevant since the issue is the credibility of Ms. F's claims about being physically and financially controlled. Although the RPD questioned Ms. F briefly about her efforts to seek police protection, her failure to report her husband was not a basis for doubting her credibility. I therefore reject Ms. F's argument that the country conditions evidence on police corruption reveal an error by the RPD. Ms. F has not challenged the RPD's other findings

The RPD found Ms. F's corroborative evidence not credible because of contradictions and internal inconsistencies. The impugned evidence included affidavits from her father and brother, and a training certificate from the Salvation Army that the RPD found was fraudulent. Ms. F has not challenged the RPD's treatment of these documents, and having independently reviewed the evidence, I see no errors in the RPD's reasons for finding these documents unreliable.

Ms. F has also not challenged the RPD's finding that her behaviour in Canada was inconsistent with that of someone who had left their children behind for either the first or second time in 6 years. Ms. F had testified that she had only told her parents she would be gone for one week, and that she made a spontaneous decision to flee her husband when the opportunity presented itself. She did not contact her children or family for 3 months because her phone was not working. The RPD, in my view, correctly, found this inconsistent with Ms. F's narrative of having only once prior left her children's side, and of leaving her children in the care of people who were expecting her return after one week. I draw a negative credibility inference. Presumption of truthfulness is rebutted

On the basis of the all of credibility concerns and uncontested findings highlighted above, I find that Ms. F's general credibility has been undermined and that the presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted. The credibility findings relate to the conditions under which Ms. F had to live during her 13 year marriage, the financial circumstances that prevented her family from repaying her dowry so she could get divorced, her family's knowledge of the abuse, and lack of contact between her and her family after she arrived in Canada. All of these factors go to the heart of Ms. F's claim for protection. Having found the credibility of these elements undermined, I find that Ms. F has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she was in a sexually or financially controlling and abusive marriage for 13 years. I find that there is no serious possibility of persecution for Ms. F in Tanzania, and I further find that she is not, on a balance of probabilities, a person in need of protection.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
